en: The Sūtra on King Brahmadatta Spoken by the Buddha;
the translator’s name is lost, now appended to the Western Jin Catalogue.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with...
He was accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a king named Brahmānanda who constantly made offerings to the Buddha and the assembly of monks.

Whenever it was a day for the uposatha fast, the king would invariably issue a command to his ministers in advance to prepare the royal carriage; the king would then lead a retinue of several thousand people to the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrate himself with his five limbs touching the ground, and bow his head at the Buddha’s feet.

Whenever the Buddha preached the sutras and the Dharma for the various devas and the people, the king would invariably listen with joy and reverence; within the royal palace as well, he served the Three Honored Ones and maintained pure fasting and precepts.

The king had a crown prince named Junlinru, who was profoundly sincere and diligent. Having realized that the world is impermanent and that there is none who does not die, he felt no attachment to worldly glory and addressed the king, saying:
"A Buddha appears in the world but rarely, and the sutras and the Dharma are difficult to hear. I now beg permission to follow the Buddha and become a śramaṇa."
The king immediately granted his request.
Jūlinru then took leave of the king and went to the Buddha’s dwelling, where he begged to become a bhikṣu.
The Buddha then stroked his head with his hand; his hair fell away and the kāṣāya robe naturally appeared upon his body.
Junlinru upheld the major precepts and practiced with diligent application, never tiring day or night; after three months, he attained the path of an Arhat.
At that time, the King was unaware that he had already attained the Way, and seeing his arduous efforts, he provided him with coarse vegetables for food.
Every time he went to make offerings, his mind was different from that of the other monks; he would invariably say to them:
"In my kingdom, there are no rare treasures of the seven jewels or delicacies of food that do not exist. Why, then, do you take such pleasure in becoming śramaṇas?"
The Buddha, knowing that the king acted out of affection, then said to Kāśyapa Mātaṅga:
"Arise and manifest your spiritual power.

Kāśyapa Mātaṅga immediately followed the Buddha’s instruction; he prostrated himself with his head to the ground to pay homage to the Buddha, then rose lightly and stayed suspended in mid-air. He manifested various transformations, flying through the air and dividing his body into many forms, passing in and out of them without obstruction. Having finished these displays, he again prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet.

When the King saw that his virtue and realization were thus, he was overcome with a mixture of grief and joy; prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he paid homage to the Brahmin Keṇiya.

The Buddha then instructed Keṇiya to explain to the King the essentials of the Four Noble Truths—suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self. Thereupon, the King’s mind was liberated, and he immediately attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"There are four matters concerning which a bhikṣu may accept the offerings of food, drink, fine flavors, and clothing from others, without incurring either merit or demerit:
first, when he intends to bring blessing upon the household that gives the gift."
Second, not wishing to act contrary to another’s intentions;
third, being either advanced in age or afflicted by physical illness;
fourth, fearing that the person on the path may undergo hardship.

Now, if one wishes to enjoy fine food, one must maintain mindfulness of the gravity of the precepts: all sentient beings have been my own kin, though through the long course of transmigration and repeated births and deaths, we have forgotten our origins.
It is like when a person has sores or illnesses on their body; they take medicine solely to effect a cure and must not harbor greedy attachment to it.
"Those who wish to give should all maintain an impartial mind, regardless of whether the gift is large or small.

Thereupon, the Buddha instructed Ānanda to recite the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (monastic precept) before the meal; as for the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, it means that the food provided to the community of monks must be entirely equal.
According to the sequence of the catalog, two sheets and eight lines are missing from all extant editions.
*The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on King Brahmadatta*.
